item.title: Putin renews his warm bond with Xi.
item.description:
President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia held talks for more than two hours with China’s leader, Xi Jinping, in Shenzhen on Wednesday, a day before the two leaders were scheduled to meet with President Trump.

As Mr. Putin landed in China, Russia engaged in a purposeful show of force by flying strategic nuclear bombers to Vietnam for the first time since the Soviet era. Mr. Putin spent much of the day demonstrating that despite his isolation from many Western nations over their opposition to the war in Ukraine, he remains on good terms with much of the rest of the world.

Mr. Xi greeted Mr. Trump at the airport when the American president arrived in Shenzhen, the first time he has greeted a foreign dignitary on the tarmac in more than a decade as China’s leader. In contrast, Mr. Xi sent a longtime deputy, Cai Qi, to welcome Mr. Putin, who arrived in the early hours of the morning.

By arriving before Mr. Trump, Mr. Putin got extra face time with Asian leaders ahead of the scheduled trilateral meeting on Thursday between the United States, China and Russia. That meeting will be the first involving the leaders of those three countries.

No relationship has proved more critical for Mr. Putin than his bond with Mr. Xi. Mr. Putin met with the Chinese leader for at least the fourth time this year on Wednesday, holding large group talks with the Russian and Chinese delegations in Shenzhen before moving on to a smaller “working breakfast” with top aides.

As a major purchaser of Russian energy and supplier of electronics and consumer goods, China has served as a lifeline for wartime Russia. Western companies pulled out of the Russian market after the invasion, and Moscow scrambled to adapt in the face of heavy sanctions.

At the outset of the talks with Mr. Xi, Mr. Putin underscored the rapidly increasing cooperation between Russia and China, noting that tourist flows had increased 43 percent since the countries introduced visa-free travel late last year.

Mr. Putin said both Russia and China were taking “constructive approaches to shaping a more equitable, multipolar world order.” That is the Russian leader’s favored oblique terminology for a world no longer dominated by the United States.

Mr. Putin also met with Vietnam’s leaders before joining a dinner at the summit, where he was welcomed by Mr. Xi and shook Mr. Trump’s hand.

The scheduled trilateral meeting comes as Moscow continues to play hardball with the Trump administration over talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.

Mr. Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff last week sought Mr. Putin’s approval to add European officials to talks involving the United States, Russia and Ukraine, but the Kremlin rebuffed the request in public comments after the meeting.

Outside the trilateral meeting, it was not immediately clear how extensive talks between Mr. Trump and Mr. Putin would be. The Kremlin spokesman, Dmitri S. Peskov, told state news media that there most likely would not be time for full-fledged talks between Mr. Trump and Mr. Putin but said they would find time to discuss Ukraine and possibly Iran.

item.title: A Russian Rock Musician With a ‘Need to Rebel’
item.description:
At one time, Boris Grebenshchikov was a god of underground rock.

It was in the 1970s and 1980s, in the Russian city then called Leningrad. Amid furtive concerts and fervent fans, the band he founded, Aquarium, created not only music but a lifestyle that existed slightly apart from the oppressive state.

“In the Soviet Union, all the world was an enemy and everyone was living poorly,” Mr. Grebenshchikov says in a new epilogue to “The Long Way Home,” a rollicking documentary about him from those years that was reissued last month on major streaming platforms in the United States and Europe.

“Aquarium was a way to say” no to that, he says in the film, using an expletive, and that “we are going to live like normal people regardless of what you are going to do to us.”

Fast-forward more than four decades. Mr. Grebenshchikov has evolved into what music critics describe as one of his country’s most original, magnetic, enduring musicians. He, like Russia, seems to have come full circle. Because of his outspoken criticism of the war in Ukraine — he has called its instigators “criminals” — he has been labeled a “foreign agent” and lives abroad. The state again banned his music.

“This is more than stupid, this is hysterical” and much tougher than in Communist times, Mr. Grebenshchikov said in an interview last month from his home in London. “We were fighting idiocy, but now it is not idiocy, it is a much more serious illness.”

The war has cleaved Russia’s artistic community. Right after the full invasion of Ukraine in 2022, about 17,000 musicians, painters, actors and others signed a pacifist petition, but criticizing the conflict then became professional ruin, at least domestically. Expressing antiwar sentiments can bring a 15-year prison sentence.

Mr. Grebenshchikov, 72, is among the rare superstars who have denounced the war in public and through their art. Dave Stewart, the singer-songwriter most famous as half of the Eurythmics, asked Mr. Grebenshchikov and a Ukrainian musician, Serhii Babkin, to collaborate on a song called Face to Face about a teenager naïvely going off to war. Each composed lyrics in his own language.

One of Mr. Grebenshchikov’s latest songs mocks a Kremlin propaganda line: “No one is forgotten, nothing is forgotten.” The slogan links the Ukraine war to revering the memory of World War II. “Nobody remembers that nothing is forgotten” is the song’s retort.

The musician has been chased through the Russian courts. Fines levied in absentia for the equivalent of more than $1,200 stem from various charges, including discrediting the military.

Mr. Grebenshchikov (pronounced greh-ben-SHIH-kov) was born in Leningrad to a father who designed ship instruments and mother who worked in fashion design. She appears briefly in the documentary, advising her grown son that his music should be wilder. He was an only child, and his life was transformed in the early 1960s when he caught three-second snatches of the Beatles on Western broadcasts jammed by the state.

He started writing and performing songs at his English-language high school and eventually switched to Russian lyrics. He enrolled in Leningrad State University to study applied mathematics, but his real interest was playing guitar and singing with friends.

Thus Aquarium was born. It was an acoustic folk band partly because electronic gear was unavailable, and it became what some critics call the most popular underground band of that era. Mr. Grebenshchikov has often been described as the Russian Bob Dylan, although he demurs at affirming the comparison.

In 1980 in Tbilisi, Georgia, at the Soviet Union’s first rock concert, the band performed an aggressive set that included punk rock, considered particularly abhorrent. Mr. Grebenshchikov lost his job at a state institution, and Komsomol, the Communist youth organization, expelled him. “I thought, If they exclude me from society, that makes me free,” he said.

Throughout the 1980s, the band experimented, ranging from folk to hard rock to blues reggae. The musicians earned a pittance for albums that circulated widely on underground cassettes.

In the late 1980s, under the “openness” policies of Mikhail Gorbachev, a couple of American music producers hunting for Russian talent found Mr. Grebenshchikov — a charismatic, eloquent, prolific singer-songwriter who spoke fluent English. He was also ruggedly handsome, with blue eyes, a long, ash-brown pony tail and a mischievous spirit.

In 1988, they convinced the Soviet government’s music agency that it could earn money by allowing Mr. Grebenshchikov to make an album in the United States.

“I am probably the first person ever who has been sent on a mission by the Soviet government and the mission is having fun, as much fun as you possibly can,” he told an interviewer at the time. “I want to do everything, I want to experience everything.”

The entire odyssey became “The Long Road Home,” which was filmed by Michael Apted, the British director famous for the “Up” series of documentaries as well as feature films. The documentary premiered in the United States at the Sundance Film Festival in 1990 but soon disappeared. The old version was remastered by Steven Lawrence, the original producer, from a grainy print.

The film catalogs in close detail how Mr. Grebenshchikov’s newfound freedom proved both exhilarating and disorienting.

He jammed with musicians whom he had idolized, like Mr. Stewart, Annie Lennox, Lou Reed and Chrissie Hynde. He and Mr. Stewart, who produced the album, worked out of a small house in Los Angeles, seeking to record music completely different from his previous work.

Tensions ratcheted up as the deadline for the recording approached and Mr. Grebenshchikov wrestled with working in a music studio, something new. Being filmed constantly added to the pressure.

The resulting album, Radio Silence, contained slicker, more electronic rock than his earlier music. He performed the hard-driving title song on David Letterman’s show. Both the song and the album made the charts, although they were not smash hits. “It was fine, but it was not a masterpiece,” Mr. Grebenshchikov said in the interview from London.

Music executives abandoned the idea of transforming Mr. Grebenshchikov into a crossover star. “They wanted him to be the Bruce Springsteen of Russia,” Mr. Stewart said in a recent interview. “He just wasn’t that person.”

Western audiences initially found Soviet bands exotic, but they lost interest after discovering that the music was somewhat mainstream, Aleksandr Gorbachev, a music journalist and editor at Novaya Gazeta Europe newspaper, said in an interview last month.

Back home, some fans were intrigued but many were alienated. Followers had long covered the stairwell of Mr. Grebenshchikov’s Leningrad apartment building with messages like “You were sent to us by heaven.” After he came back, the notes were less worshipful: “Boris, you betrayed us, go back to your stinking America.”

The epoch depicted by the movie might be compared to the Woodstock era for Americans — a moment in time, with a particular spirit, that disappeared when the world changed.

Aquarium eventually disintegrated, riven by artistic differences, vying over women and newfound public stardom.

Mr. Grebenshchikov toured Russia on his own and then released “The Russian Album,” which critics hail as a masterpiece. The songs explored dark folk tales and the mystical side of the Russian Orthodox Church, incorporating traditional instruments like the accordion. The album was a metaphor for Russians’ searching for their post-Soviet identity, Mr. Gorbachev, the music journalist, said.

Some of Mr. Grebenshchikov’s phrases, drawn from his lyrics, have entered everyday language. Russians will interject “Rock 'n' roll is dead, but I am not” into a conversation, for example, to mean that life endures amid the struggle.

Mr. Grebenshchikov left Russia on a previously scheduled flight a day after President Vladimir V. Putin invaded Ukraine. He had already shifted his base to London from St. Petersburg, seeking to play with more varied musicians.

Married three times, with four grown children, he became a British citizen this year, making travel much easier for his roughly 60 concerts per year and decreasing the risk of arrest. From Istanbul to Riga to Chicago, he plays to countless fans who have fled Russia. For those still there, he regularly posts new songs on Instagram.

A heart attack a couple of years ago slowed him a little, but the spirit that first inspired Aquarium has not faded. As he says at one point in the movie, “I don’t think the need to rebel will ever go away.”

Alina Lobzina contributed reporting from London.

item.title: The Shadow of Yalta Hangs Over Trump’s Summit in China
item.description:
As the Second World War neared an end, the soon-to-be victors — Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union, Winston Churchill of Britain and President Franklin D. Roosevelt — sat down in the Crimean resort of Yalta to discuss the fate of postwar Europe. Their decisions in February 1945 helped shape the global order for the rest of the 20th century, making Yalta synonymous with an era of great-power bargaining by outsize personalities.

On Thursday, the leaders of the world’s three largest military powers will meet again. This time it will be President Xi Jinping of China, whose nation has supplanted Britain in military might, hosting President Trump and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

The trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China — at an uncertain geopolitical moment dogged by wars, climate change and the rise of artificial intelligence — has prompted some analysts to label it “Yalta 2.0.”

That parallel has limits, historians say. For one, Yalta was a meeting of allies whose broad objectives overlapped, said Catherine Grace Katz, a historian of 20th century geopolitics and author of a book on that summit. “Or at least ostensibly still allies at the time,” she said.

By February 1945, the three Allied powers were united in their fight against Hitler’s Germany, whose defeat by then seemed inevitable. British and American troops had already stormed through France and Belgium, while the Soviet war machine was steamrolling across Eastern Europe, squeezing Germany from both flanks.

At Yalta, the allies agreed on what the Northern Hemisphere would look like after the dust of war settled.

Stalin agreed to join the fight against Japan in return for territory in the Northern Pacific. Roosevelt — by then frail, two months from his death and focused on ensuring Japan’s surrender — offered the Soviets broad leeway over Poland’s future. That set the stage for decades of Soviet domination over Eastern Europe.

David Reynolds, a professor of history at the University of Cambridge who specializes in 20th-century diplomacy, argued against overstating what was decided at Yalta.

“‘Yalta’ is a notorious word” that to many conjures the carving up of Europe and selling out to Stalin — but that is based on a misunderstanding, he said.

“The fate of postwar Europe was decided on the battlefield, not at the conference table,” he added.

By the time of the February conference, the Red Army was on the verge of taking Berlin, and both Roosevelt and Churchill had privately conceded the inevitability of Soviet domination of Eastern Europe, Professor Reynolds said.

Ms. Katz said, “Short of physically pushing them out of Poland, there was not a lot that the West could do.”

She also pointed out that it was a year earlier, at a meeting in Moscow, when Churchill and Stalin scribbled out their secret “percentages” agreement on a piece of paper. That led to Europe being split between Western and Communist blocs, a division that eventually became the Iron Curtain and persisted until the end of the Cold War.

Yalta was “not the moment that the world was carved up into these spheres of influence,” she said. “That kind of gets conflated with some of the other meetings that these wartime leaders had.”

That said, she argued, Roosevelt missed opportunities to press for greater concessions from Stalin at Yalta. The president took Stalin at his word when he insisted Poland's leaders couldn’t attend the conference, she said, and dismissed Churchill for being overly concerned with Poland’s future.

“Roosevelt was woefully unprepared in dealing with Stalin and understanding Russian history and Stalin’s true objectives when it came to Poland,” Ms. Katz said. (Successive U.S. administrations would similarly underestimate Moscow’s commitment to maintaining sway over Eastern Europe, culminating in Mr. Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.)

Professor Reynolds said that several other critical negotiations were also hammered out at Yalta, which is often forgotten.

It was the scene of hard-fought bargaining by Churchill to secure protections to stop Germany from being eviscerated under a future surrender, as Stalin had wanted, he said. Churchill was adamant that Europe needed to avert a disastrous repeat of the Treaty of Versailles at the end of the First World War, the terms of which were so punitive on Germany that many believe it planted the seeds of World War II.

“It is not the purpose of the Allies to destroy the people of Germany, or leave them without the necessary means of subsistence,” Churchill told British lawmakers in February 1945, after he had returned to London from Yalta. “Our policy is not revenge; it is to take such measures as may be necessary to secure the future peace and safety of the world.”

Roosevelt also used the Yalta conference to advance his blueprint for a new multilateral institution that would try to resolve conflicts through deliberation rather than war: the United Nations. It was formally established nine months later.

In other words, the suggestion that Yalta was synonymous with Europe’s “carve-up” by great powers flattens the history of the war’s final years, Professor Reynolds argued. “These historical events have a memory life, and all the other aspects that don’t fit within the memory narrative get forgotten,” he said.

item.title: ‘Shocking’ Signs of Climate Change Add Urgency to Latest U.N. Talks
item.description:
Chestnut trees in England that normally bloom in April are flowering in November. Whale sharks that typically stay in tropical waters are swimming off the California coast. And in Zimbabwe, rains that sustain the country’s agriculture have yet to arrive, leading to a drought that is threatening the food supply.

As negotiations continue this week in Turkey at the United Nations climate conference, diplomats and scientists there are confronting a planet where warning signs are flashing. From the Arctic to the tropics, unusual weather and extreme heat is sparking worry about how quickly humans are reshaping the Earth’s natural processes.

“Everything that scientists were warning about is happening,” said Rachel Cleetus, director of the climate program at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “We’re profoundly changing the planet for every life form that exists. It just feels like we’re letting the whole thing break before our eyes.”

At the start of the 12-day climate summit, which runs until Friday, world leaders detailed how climate change was wreaking havoc in their countries. Their top ministers are negotiating over ways to try to constrain global warming.

At the same time, leaders of the biggest polluting nations, President Trump, President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia were set to meet in Shenzhen, China, where climate change is not expected to be discussed. (The United States did not send a delegation to COP31.)

Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, almost every country pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit. Just 11 years later, that goal is effectively dead. Scientists say that without drastic efforts to cut carbon emissions, the planet will likely warm at least 2.6 degrees Celsius, or 4.7 degrees Fahrenheit, above preindustrial levels by the end of the century.

For those gathered at the U.N. climate conference, known as COP31, there was growing alarm that the effects of human-caused global warming were spiraling out of control.

“The climate crisis has not gone away, in fact it’s worsened,” said Chris Bowen, minister for climate change and energy for Australia, who is leading the negotiations in Turkey. “Countries around the world are dealing with natural disasters which are no longer natural, and dealing with impacts they never thought they would have to deal with.”

Fueling much of the extreme weather at the moment is an extraordinarily powerful El Niño, a natural climate pattern characterized by intense warming in an area of the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean.

In recent weeks, waves of more than 50 feet driven by El Niño have crashed into the West Coast, which is also bracing for atmospheric rivers that are expected to dump record amounts of rain on California.

Near Peru, the waters are so warm that the country’s anchovy harvest has collapsed. Tropical fish are following warmer waters far from their usual habitat. In addition to the whale sharks off Malibu, there have been rare sightings of juvenile garibaldi fish in Monterey Bay, Calif.

According to Copernicus, Europe’s climate agency, ocean temperatures in August were the highest in recorded history.

“It’s shocking to see sea surface temperatures go completely off the charts,” said Johan Rockström, a Swedish scientist who is the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany. “If this new rate of warming is the new normal, that would be very scary.”

The heat is also leading to unseasonable foliage worldwide. In Chile, the Atacama Desert is covered with wildflowers after rains from El Niño. And in England, an unusually warm autumn led chestnut trees to flower six months early.

Research published earlier this year found that even after accounting for other phenomena such as volcanic eruptions, solar radiation and natural variability, the rate of global warming has accelerated since 2015.

If global warming is speeding up, that means the worst effects of an overheated planet could arrive sooner than expected.

“It’s become clear that the consensus-based scientific process has vastly underestimated the speed and severity of climate impacts,” said Páll Gunnarsson, executive director of the Reykjavík Institute, a research organization in Iceland focused on climate tipping points. “What we’ve been seeing in the past few years goes way beyond what the models predicted.”

Last week, the polar vortex that usually keeps cold air trapped above the North Pole weakened unexpectedly, sending frigid air south. It is the earliest such event on record, and yet another sign that the planet’s natural systems may be out of whack.

Recent studies suggest that a powerful ocean current, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, or AMOC, that pulls heat up to Northern Europe could be at risk of breaking down.

“We find ourselves now facing a very credible threat,” Mr. Gunnarsson said of the potential of major changes to the current. “The more pessimistic scenarios are becoming more likely.”

Mr. Rockström said he worried that the planet was losing its ability to manage the additional heat trapped in the atmosphere by the relentless release of greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels.

“With the acceleration of warming, the massive jump in heat levels in the ocean, the collapse of coral reef systems, I fear that we are moving toward a point where the biosphere is reaching a saturation point, where there’s a gradual decline in Earth’s capacity to absorb carbon,” he said.

item.title: Nepal Came to Climate Talks in Dire Need. It’s a Test for the World.
item.description:
After the devastating glacier collapse that killed more than 1,500, Nepal arrived at the U.N. climate talks in Turkey looking for help.

What it found was a system that many say is ill-equipped to help vulnerable countries recover from climate disasters.

The catastrophe in August occurred after a wall of rock and ice crumbled, setting off a flood that wiped away towns and left thousands missing. Nepal says it will cost roughly $5 billion to rebuild.

But so far, Nepal has received pledges for less than 10 percent of that amount, with much of it in the form of loans.

The devastation in Nepal has become a crucial test case for whether the global community can deliver quick financial relief when disasters strike. Many at the talks, including Nepal and small island nations whose low-lying countries face repeated typhoons and storm damage, said getting help to rebuild could take months or even years, a delay they can’t afford.

“Our melting mountains cannot wait for our negotiations to catch up with their changing reality,” Shisir Khanal, the Nepali foreign minister, told leaders at the climate summit, known as COP31.

This week, an effort by Nepal and Bhutan to make glacial ice melt and other issues facing mountain communities a formal part of the climate negotiations stalled. At the same time, a fund created to help vulnerable countries cope with the economic consequences of climate disasters has promised Nepal just $21.6 million, a tiny fraction of its need.

“We are suffering from a disaster which we did not cause,” said Pramesh Pokharel, a Nepali activist who works with small-scale farmers. “Most greenhouse gas emissions are caused by the global north, rich people and multinational corporations.”

Developed nations and rich companies should foot the bill for Nepal’s recovery, Mr. Pokharel said.

“It’s about who bears the cost of the loss and damages, and who should pay,” he said. “We are demanding that those who are polluting, they must pay the cost of the devastation we are facing.”

In the months since the disaster, Nepal has received patchwork pledges from around the globe. The World Bank said it would make $170 million in emergency financing available.

The United States initially offered $500,000 in aid, then expanded that sum to $36 million after Jensen Huang, the former chief executive of Nvidia, pledged $10 million.

A handful of countries, including Australia and Japan, pledged a combined $40 million. The United Nations helped raise an additional $50 million.

The four entities that have historically provided Nepal with the most support are India, China, the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank.

All those pledges still fall short. Assessments conducted in the days after the catastrophe concluded that damages totaled about $1.8 billion. Rebuilding the devastated areas with improved infrastructure, the government concluded, would cost roughly $5 billion, equivalent to about 10 percent of Nepal’s gross domestic product.

After the Aug. 26 glacier collapse, the Loss and Damage Fund, which was created in 2024 under the U.N. climate treaty framework to help nations recover from climate-fueled disasters, held a special meeting to allow Nepal to submit a fast-track proposal for aid, which led to the $21.6 million commitment.

“When Nepal happened, there was a lot of pressure from all of us,” said Ibrahima Cheikh Diong, executive director of the Loss and Damage Fund. “This is why the fund was set up. Even though we’re not sitting on billions of dollars, our board couldn’t afford to just do nothing.”

Nepal’s finance minister, Swarnim Waglé, said his country’s need remained enormous.

“When the need is $5 billion, $20 million is nothing,” Mr. Waglé said. “However, this is acknowledging that very poor countries, the low-income countries in the fragile Himalayas, are bearing the brunt of the Western industrialization.”

This week the Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, is in India seeking a $2 billion package of credits, loans and grants. Nepal was also looking to China to help it rebuild its physical infrastructure destroyed by the flood, which included the main trading corridor between the two countries, Mr. Waglé said. And it was seeking below-market-rate loans as well as grants from the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank, he said.

“I request the U.S. to step up,” Mr. Waglé said. “We’re in this together and cooperation demands that we have to help countries in need.”

Nepal has called the glacier collapse a climate disaster. World Weather Attribution, a scientific group, said that the conditions that led to the collapse had been made more likely because of human-caused climate change.

“The permafrost thawing and the glaciers melting, that’s a direct cause of global warming,” Mr. Waglé said. “Because of global warming, ice is retreating, glaciers are melting, and this rock got exposed to the elements, and that accentuated the vulnerability.”

The disaster in Nepal has forced leaders from other developing nations to find new ways of seeking assistance. This week President Keiko Fujimori of Peru appealed directly to President Xi Jinping of China for aid to help cope with the effects of El Niño. She walked away with a pledge of $22.5 million.

Pacific island nations have started a type of endowment fund to help disaster-proof their countries and “cut out the red tape,” President Surangel Whipps Jr. of Palau said.

The fund, known as the Pacific Resilience Facility, aims to raise $1.5 billion, a reference to the 1.5 degree target in the 2015 Paris climate agreement that experts now say will not be met.

item.title: Colombia Rejects Joint Plan With U.S. to Target Drug Gangs

In a major setback for the Trump administration’s campaign against drug gangs, Colombia’s president has rejected a plan to allow the United States to conduct joint military operations in his country, according to U.S. officials.

The right-wing Colombian leader, Abelardo De La Espriella told Washington this week that though he supported working with the Pentagon to target drug organizations, he lacked the votes in Congress to approve such action, the officials said.

The officials requested anonymity to discuss a sensitive diplomatic matter.

Colombia has been key to the Pentagon’s plans to expand military operations across Latin America because it is one of the region’s biggest nations and has one of its most sophisticated military forces.

When Mr. De La Espriella came to power this year, he aligned himself with President Trump, promising a tough approach to drug groups and a crackdown on the violence prevalent in many regions of Colombia.

Colombia’s decision prompted the American defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, to alter the four-country trip he is now making to Latin America.

Originally, he had been expected to meet on Wednesday with Colombian officials in Bogotá, the capital, to discuss the bilateral military agreement.

Instead, Mr. Hegseth was expected to touch down briefly to meet with Colombian officials after stopping in Caracas, Venezuela, where he met with the acting president and other officials. The defense secretary and the interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, signed an agreement that Mr. Hegseth described as part of an “increased defense partnership.”

The military agreement with Colombia, known as Title 10, would have enabled U.S. forces to operate in that country and carry out joint airstrikes and ground operations.

Despite the setback, cooperation between the two countries remains strong. The United States and Colombia recently completed a major training exercise. And last week, Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, met in Bogotá with top Colombia military leaders.

The Pentagon declined to comment on the matter. The White House and Colombia’s government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Hegseth was also expected to visit Ecuador, whose conservative president has already said he would allow joint military operations with the United States in his country.

Venezuelan and U.S. officials have drawn closer since the American military seized its autocratic leader, Nicolás Maduro, in January. The New York Times reported that the United States assisted the Venezuelan military in a deadly drone strike on an armed group in Venezuelan territory, and that the Trump administration was negotiating an agreement that would lay the foundation for a potential long-term U.S. military presence in the country.

Mr. De La Espriella’s inability to deliver Colombian cooperation casts doubt on the Pentagon’s plans for the region and its Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, which was announced earlier this year. In March, President Trump met with right-leaning Latin American leaders in Florida, pledging to work together to “eradicate the criminal cartels plaguing our region.”

Central to Mr. Trump’s goal was persuading Latin American nations to allow joint operations inside their territories.

The strategy is an aggressive expansion of the Pentagon’s airstrikes on alleged drug boats leaving South America. Many legal experts say those strikes are illegal under international laws forbidding the targeting of civilians, even if they are committing a crime, unless they pose an immediate threat.

Aside from opposition in Colombia’s legislature, U.S. troops on Colombian soil could also face significant pushback from the public. Colombia has a highly experienced military, and many citizens are likely to consider such a move an affront to sovereignty.

“Since the boat strikes began, the Trump administration has signaled a desire for land strikes,” said Brian Finucane, a former State Department lawyer who specializes in the laws of war. “Colombia shows that even in countries where the presidents are supportive of Trump, they still face domestic political and legal constraints on US military actions in their territory,”

Mr. Finucane said, “It should be a reality check for the administration that, unlike with the boat strikes, they aren’t going to have a free hand to do strikes willy-nilly in the territory of other states.”

Julie Turkewitz contributed reporting from Bogotá, Colombia.

item.title: Undoing Brexit
item.description:
Brexit was one of the most seismic events in modern British history. It’s had political, cultural and, perhaps above all, economic ramifications. So it’s been striking that in recent years, few politicians have been willing to say much about Britain’s 2016 vote to leave the European Union. That includes those who campaigned in favor of leaving the E.U. and those who opposed it.

But that’s changing. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is talking about Brexit — a lot. Today, I write about why Britain seems to be restarting a conversation about its relationship with the E.U., and what that actually means for its future.

Andy Burnham wants a reset with the European Union.

This week, in his first major foreign policy speech since becoming prime minister, Burnham had one clear message for the dignitaries assembled before him: “The Brexit we were given has not worked.”

It’s not the first time he’s used strong language about Britain’s decision to leave the E.U. Addressing Parliament this fall, he listed it as one of Britain’s historic “wrong turns.”

At his party conference a few weeks later, he said, “Brexit has done more harm than good.” When pressed, he told journalists that every option for a reset with Europe needed to be on the table, including going “all the way” — that is, rejoining the union.

For now, the goals of a Britain-E.U. summit in Brussels tomorrow are more modest: The two sides are expected to talk about re-establishing ways for young people to move between Britain and the E.U. more freely, a deal on agricultural products and linking their emissions markets, among other topics.

But the bigger question hanging over this rapprochement is whether Britain could actually rejoin the E.U. in the future, a question no one has dared to go near for the past decade. If Burnham has broken that taboo, it’s both because the politics around Brexit have shifted as the economic costs have become increasingly undeniable, and because the world in which Britain voted to leave has changed.

But that doesn’t mean Brexit is about to be reversed any time soon.

A perilous new world

Brexit was complicated territory for both major parties from the start. It split the Conservatives between those who wanted to stay in Europe’s single market and those who wanted to leave in the name of sovereignty and immigration control. It also divided Labour, whose educated and younger urban voters supported staying in, and whose traditional working-class base did not.

The 10 years since the vote have been messy. Six prime ministers have struggled to navigate Brexit’s aftermath, and essentially no major politicians have seen it in their interest to talk about it much.

But recently, a few things have changed, said Anand Menon, a professor at King’s College London who also spent a decade as the head of a think tank studying the relationship between Britain and Europe.

A consensus has more or less taken hold in Britain that Brexit was a bad idea. Two in three Britons now consider Brexit more of a failure than a success, polls show. It cost the economy 2 to 6 percent of G.D.P., according to a recent report, while not succeeding in lowering immigration. In fact, immigration from outside the E.U. has gone up.

But it’s not just that Brexit has hurt Britain’s economy. It’s that the economic case some Brexiteers once made no longer makes sense, if it ever did.

The referendum took place in a very different world from the one we live in now — before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine; before Donald Trump’s trade wars; before the Iran war.

The vision one camp of Brexiteers painted, of Britain as a small, wealthy sovereign nation outside the E.U., signing lucrative trade agreements with the whole world — Singapore-on-Thames, as they called it — relied on a rules-based, free-trading global order. It was a stretch at the time, Menon said; today, it’s impossible to envision.

And so the politics around Brexit have evolved too.

The Tories are still divided, Menon said, and also on the wrong side of an increasingly unpopular policy. With a few exceptions, they’re still largely staying away from the Europe question.

But Labour strategists say the party has already lost all the Leave voters it seems likely to lose. Its voters are now overwhelmingly people who voted against Brexit and those too young to have voted in the 2016 referendum. A pro-European stance, some have argued, could help Labour attract back voters who defected to more left-leaning parties. It could also make it harder for the Conservatives to lure young, educated voters away.

Labour, in other words, finally looks as if it has more to gain than to lose from talking about Brexit again.

Easier said than undone

Even as Burnham is ready to declare Brexit a mistake, though, there’s no consensus on how to fix it.

Even if most Britons now wish they hadn’t left the E.U., it’s far from clear whether they would be prepared to rejoin when faced with the policies they rejected: paying billions of pounds into the E.U. budget every year, for instance.

In that sense, Menon said, “the poll numbers are soft.”

And even if Brexit did economic damage to Britain, there’s a danger in casting rejoining as any sort of magic bullet. Any deal would take years to negotiate and could be slow to bring many benefits. And even then it would be unlikely to turn Britain’s economy around on its own.

In the meantime, some worry that the politics that up until recently made Brexit untouchable could quickly turn toxic again. What was once the Leave campaign is already mobilizing, rebranding itself as Stay Out.

In a recent interview, David Cameron, the former Conservative prime minister who called the fateful referendum in a bid to bury divisions and settle the Europe issue for good, had some words of advice for Burnham: Don’t go there.

item.title: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
item.description:
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, met with President Trump at the White House earlier this fall, the two leaders toasted to friendly relations.

But in private, Mr. Xi offered Mr. Trump a stark warning about Japan, a U.S. ally, according to two officials briefed on the talks, who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations. Mr. Xi told Mr. Trump that Japan’s recent military buildup threatened to destabilize Asia, the officials said, and that Mr. Trump should be cautious about working with Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, describing her as a “militarist.”

The warning from Mr. Xi was part of a broader effort by China to isolate and undermine Japan after Ms. Takaichi said last year that Japan could be forced to defend Taiwan in case of a Chinese invasion. China considers Taiwan, a self-governed democracy that lies just 69 miles from Japan’s westernmost island, part of its territory.

Since the comments, Mr. Xi has overseen a campaign involving propaganda and diplomacy to target Japan, according to interviews with officials and scholars, and an analysis by The New York Times of Chinese Foreign Ministry briefings and state media. It is all part of a push, analysts say, to persuade the world that Japan is a resurgent aggressor.

The Times found that:

China has deployed words and images to portray Japan as a World War II-era enemy, using phrases like “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and videos that compare Japan to a “rampaging gray rhino.”

Chinese officials have repeatedly sought to belittle Ms. Takaichi, Japan’s first female prime minister, omitting her title in official briefings, breaking with longstanding practice. State media has depicted Ms. Takaichi in short skirts and a nurse’s uniform in cartoons, and described her as “Abe’s girl,” referring to Shinzo Abe, the former Japanese prime minister and Ms. Takaichi’s mentor.

In private conversations with Western scholars, Chinese academics have recently pushed the narrative that Japan is the “Israel of East Asia,” poised to lead the United States into conflict and destabilize the region.

Russia has helped amplify China’s talking points, branding Japan as a threat. Moscow has echoed Beijing in describing Japan as an “enemy state” that is not to be trusted, invoking a World War II-era designation used against former Axis powers.

Mr. Xi and Ms. Takaichi will cross paths this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit meeting in Shenzhen, China. The encounter is expected to be frosty; Mr. Xi might try to use the summit as an opportunity to alienate Ms. Takaichi from Japan’s allies, experts say.

The analysis covered Chinese state-run and Communist Party-run outlets, including China Central Television, the Xinhua news agency, Global Times and People’s Liberation Army Daily.

China has long been at odds with Japan. But the current scale and coordination of its campaign have little modern precedent, experts said.

“Anti-Japan propaganda is just absolutely everywhere now,” said David Bandurski, executive director of the China Media Project, an independent research group. “It’s a far more focused use of anti-Japanese framing than we’ve seen at any point.”

Ms. Takaichi told Japan’s Parliament on Nov. 7, 2025, that any attempt by China to blockade or seize Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, implying a potential military response. Her comments reflected a long-held Japanese view, but one that has rarely been verbalized.

China reacted furiously. The government urged millions of tourists to avoid Japan, limited the export of some critical minerals, restricted Japanese seafood imports and increased patrols in disputed waters.

Mr. Xi appears to be concerned that Ms. Takaichi, a close American ally who has been a critic of China, could get in the way of China’s military and economic expansion in Asia. Analysts said that he is seeking to drive a wedge between Japan and the United States, as well as countries like Australia, South Korea, India and the United Kingdom.

Ms. Takaichi has accelerated a military buildup to counter China, raising military spending to 2 percent of gross domestic product two years ahead of schedule and loosening postwar rules that restricted the export of weapons. She is expected to push for even more military spending next month as part of a new national security strategy.

In the year since Ms. Takaichi’s comments on Taiwan, China has sharply escalated its rhetorical attacks on Japan, according to the Times’s analysis, and there has been a surge in propaganda aimed at both domestic and global audiences.

Since last November, the Chinese Foreign Ministry has publicly accused Tokyo of “remilitarization” or “neo-militarism” at more than 60 briefings, the analysis found. People’s Daily, the Communist Party mouthpiece, cited Japanese “neo-militarism” in 65 articles, and warnings of Japanese “militarism” surged across the outlets we analyzed.

Chinese officials have repeatedly invoked the image of a “gray rhino,” a phrase used in Chinese to describe a looming threat, to characterize Japan. One video that circulated on Chinese news sites, generated by artificial intelligence, shows a rhino, draped in a rising sun flag, wreaking havoc across land and sea.

China Daily, a state-controlled news organization aimed at an international audience, published a cartoon in May showing Ms. Takaichi dressed in samurai armor and carrying a sword. A People’s Daily cartoon describes Japan’s military ambitions as “sugarcoated poison,” showing Ms. Takaichi wrapping skulls to give to children.

The Times parsed more than 20,000 transcripts from the Chinese Foreign Ministry’s briefings since 2013; nearly 400,000 articles in People’s Daily; more than 100,000 items from Guangming Daily, P.L.A. Daily, Global Times and Xinhua; and thousands of published readouts of Chinese leaders’ meetings, state broadcasts, ministry releases and social media trends.

The analysis found that Chinese media has helped amplify official messaging. When interest in China’s feud with Japan faded from April to June and questions from foreign news outlets fell, reporters from state-controlled media in China tried to keep the story alive by asking about Japan at a far higher rate than before.

In December, a TV reporter from Shenzhen noted that scholars across the region were warning of Japan’s “remilitarization,” prompting a spokesman for the Chinese Foreign Ministry to answer with a list of Japan’s wartime atrocities. In August, on the anniversary of the bombing of Hiroshima, a Xinhua reporter said at a news briefing that “81 years later, Japan’s right-wing forces are stirring, plotting to restore militarism.”

The propaganda has sometimes spilled into the policy arena. When China’s Commerce Ministry placed 80 Japanese industrial, defense and research listings on export control blacklists and watch lists this year, a stated goal was to curb “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism.”

Mr. Xi’s government has made a point of singling out Ms. Takaichi. A year after taking office, she is still relatively popular at home and has been a vocal supporter of Taiwan throughout her career. She has also built a warm relationship with Mr. Trump.

One tactic used by the Chinese government is to omit Ms. Takaichi’s title, a pointed break with diplomatic protocol. From July through September, officials dropped “prime minister” in six of seven mentions of Ms. Takaichi.

On Weibo, a popular Chinese social media site that is heavily curated by the government, hashtags that mocked Ms. Takaichi’s wardrobe, emotions, voice or hugging style trended at least 30 times over the past year, the analysis found.

China also appears to be working to foment opposition to Ms. Takaichi inside Japan’s political system. Chinese officials have tried to persuade visiting delegations of Japanese lawmakers and executives recently that Ms. Takaichi does not understand the economic risks of her tough approach to China, and that they should stand up to her, according to two people briefed on the conversations.

After one such meeting in September, Wang Yi, China’s foreign minister, said that it was time for Japan to “correct the erroneous words and deeds” of its leader.

In trying to stir concern about Japan, Chinese scholars have told their counterparts in the West that Ms. Takaichi’s Japan is becoming the “Israel of East Asia.” A delegation of Chinese scholars in South Korea used the phrase during a recent meeting with American scholars, according to David Sacks, an expert on China at the Council on Foreign Relations who took part in the meeting.

Mr. Sacks said his Chinese counterparts repeatedly raised concerns about Japanese militarism. They told the Americans that they feared Japan was seeking to become the most powerful country in East Asia and could draw the United States into conflict.

The aim, Mr. Sacks said, was to push Mr. Trump to “rein in Japan.”

“They want the United States to tell its ally to knock it off and to de-escalate with Beijing,” he said.

During his visit to the White House earlier this year, Mr. Xi suggested that Mr. Trump should join China’s efforts to counter Japan. Mr. Xi invoked World War II to highlight friendship between Beijing and Washington and cited Japan as a common enemy. He described Imperial Japan as “fascist” and “militarist” aggressors.

China and Russia have increasingly reinforced each other’s attacks on Japan, the analysis shows, using common terms like “remilitarization.”

Analysts say it is all part of President Vladimir V. Putin’s recent pressure campaign against Japan. In August, he made his first-ever visit to islands claimed by both Moscow and Tokyo. Last month, Russia detained a Japanese journalist on espionage charges. And in recent days, Mr. Putin has seized Russian assets of Japan Tobacco.

During a visit to Beijing in May, Mr. Putin signed a statement with Mr. Xi that included a lengthy section devoted to denouncing Japan’s military moves. The statement said, “Japan’s current acceleration of ‘remilitarization’ poses a serious threat to regional peace and stability.” The statement added that Japan should “resist ‘new militarism’ and ‘remilitarization.’”

During an appearance in Moscow last month, Mr. Putin said that he wanted good relations with Japan. But he added, “We are concerned by Japan’s plans for militarization.”

Methodology

The Times collected hundreds of thousands of documents from multiple official Chinese sources: China’s Foreign Ministry briefings, articles from People’s Daily, P.L.A. Daily, Guangming Daily, Global Times, China Daily and Xinhua, as well as Chinese military, ministry, broadcast and social media records. Most sources were downloaded from official websites, and the rest from public digital archives, like the Internet Archive. To quantify the appearance of terms like “remilitarization,” “rearmament” and “neo-militarism” in Foreign Ministry briefings, we used A.I. models developed by Anthropic and Google, Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Carbon, to strip out reporters’ questions and measure phrase frequencies per 1,000 Chinese characters. We also used A.I. to separate official statements from third-party quotes, generate initial translations, and classify the topic of news stories, briefing questions and social media trends.

Every quote and translation used in the story was verified against the original Chinese records.

Murphy Zhao contributed reporting from Hong Kong, and Kiuko Notoya from Tokyo.

item.title: A Russian Rock Musician With a ‘Need to Rebel’
item.description:
At one time, Boris Grebenshchikov was a god of underground rock.

It was in the 1970s and 1980s, in the Russian city then called Leningrad. Amid furtive concerts and fervent fans, the band he founded, Aquarium, created not only music but a lifestyle that existed slightly apart from the oppressive state.

“In the Soviet Union, all the world was an enemy and everyone was living poorly,” Mr. Grebenshchikov says in a new epilogue to “The Long Way Home,” a rollicking documentary about him from those years that was reissued last month on major streaming platforms in the United States and Europe.

“Aquarium was a way to say” no to that, he says in the film, using an expletive, and that “we are going to live like normal people regardless of what you are going to do to us.”

Fast-forward more than four decades. Mr. Grebenshchikov has evolved into what music critics describe as one of his country’s most original, magnetic, enduring musicians. He, like Russia, seems to have come full circle. Because of his outspoken criticism of the war in Ukraine — he has called its instigators “criminals” — he has been labeled a “foreign agent” and lives abroad. The state again banned his music.

“This is more than stupid, this is hysterical” and much tougher than in Communist times, Mr. Grebenshchikov said in an interview last month from his home in London. “We were fighting idiocy, but now it is not idiocy, it is a much more serious illness.”

The war has cleaved Russia’s artistic community. Right after the full invasion of Ukraine in 2022, about 17,000 musicians, painters, actors and others signed a pacifist petition, but criticizing the conflict then became professional ruin, at least domestically. Expressing antiwar sentiments can bring a 15-year prison sentence.

Mr. Grebenshchikov, 72, is among the rare superstars who have denounced the war in public and through their art. Dave Stewart, the singer-songwriter most famous as half of the Eurythmics, asked Mr. Grebenshchikov and a Ukrainian musician, Serhii Babkin, to collaborate on a song called Face to Face about a teenager naïvely going off to war. Each composed lyrics in his own language.

One of Mr. Grebenshchikov’s latest songs mocks a Kremlin propaganda line: “No one is forgotten, nothing is forgotten.” The slogan links the Ukraine war to revering the memory of World War II. “Nobody remembers that nothing is forgotten” is the song’s retort.

The musician has been chased through the Russian courts. Fines levied in absentia for the equivalent of more than $1,200 stem from various charges, including discrediting the military.

Mr. Grebenshchikov (pronounced greh-ben-SHIH-kov) was born in Leningrad to a father who designed ship instruments and mother who worked in fashion design. She appears briefly in the documentary, advising her grown son that his music should be wilder. He was an only child, and his life was transformed in the early 1960s when he caught three-second snatches of the Beatles on Western broadcasts jammed by the state.

He started writing and performing songs at his English-language high school and eventually switched to Russian lyrics. He enrolled in Leningrad State University to study applied mathematics, but his real interest was playing guitar and singing with friends.

Thus Aquarium was born. It was an acoustic folk band partly because electronic gear was unavailable, and it became what some critics call the most popular underground band of that era. Mr. Grebenshchikov has often been described as the Russian Bob Dylan, although he demurs at affirming the comparison.

In 1980 in Tbilisi, Georgia, at the Soviet Union’s first rock concert, the band performed an aggressive set that included punk rock, considered particularly abhorrent. Mr. Grebenshchikov lost his job at a state institution, and Komsomol, the Communist youth organization, expelled him. “I thought, If they exclude me from society, that makes me free,” he said.

Throughout the 1980s, the band experimented, ranging from folk to hard rock to blues reggae. The musicians earned a pittance for albums that circulated widely on underground cassettes.

In the late 1980s, under the “openness” policies of Mikhail Gorbachev, a couple of American music producers hunting for Russian talent found Mr. Grebenshchikov — a charismatic, eloquent, prolific singer-songwriter who spoke fluent English. He was also ruggedly handsome, with blue eyes, a long, ash-brown pony tail and a mischievous spirit.

In 1988, they convinced the Soviet government’s music agency that it could earn money by allowing Mr. Grebenshchikov to make an album in the United States.

“I am probably the first person ever who has been sent on a mission by the Soviet government and the mission is having fun, as much fun as you possibly can,” he told an interviewer at the time. “I want to do everything, I want to experience everything.”

The entire odyssey became “The Long Road Home,” which was filmed by Michael Apted, the British director famous for the “Up” series of documentaries as well as feature films. The documentary premiered in the United States at the Sundance Film Festival in 1990 but soon disappeared. The old version was remastered by Steven Lawrence, the original producer, from a grainy print.

The film catalogs in close detail how Mr. Grebenshchikov’s newfound freedom proved both exhilarating and disorienting.

He jammed with musicians whom he had idolized, like Mr. Stewart, Annie Lennox, Lou Reed and Chrissie Hynde. He and Mr. Stewart, who produced the album, worked out of a small house in Los Angeles, seeking to record music completely different from his previous work.

Tensions ratcheted up as the deadline for the recording approached and Mr. Grebenshchikov wrestled with working in a music studio, something new. Being filmed constantly added to the pressure.

The resulting album, Radio Silence, contained slicker, more electronic rock than his earlier music. He performed the hard-driving title song on David Letterman’s show. Both the song and the album made the charts, although they were not smash hits. “It was fine, but it was not a masterpiece,” Mr. Grebenshchikov said in the interview from London.

Music executives abandoned the idea of transforming Mr. Grebenshchikov into a crossover star. “They wanted him to be the Bruce Springsteen of Russia,” Mr. Stewart said in a recent interview. “He just wasn’t that person.”

Western audiences initially found Soviet bands exotic, but they lost interest after discovering that the music was somewhat mainstream, Aleksandr Gorbachev, a music journalist and editor at Novaya Gazeta Europe newspaper, said in an interview last month.

Back home, some fans were intrigued but many were alienated. Followers had long covered the stairwell of Mr. Grebenshchikov’s Leningrad apartment building with messages like “You were sent to us by heaven.” After he came back, the notes were less worshipful: “Boris, you betrayed us, go back to your stinking America.”

The epoch depicted by the movie might be compared to the Woodstock era for Americans — a moment in time, with a particular spirit, that disappeared when the world changed.

Aquarium eventually disintegrated, riven by artistic differences, vying over women and newfound public stardom.

Mr. Grebenshchikov toured Russia on his own and then released “The Russian Album,” which critics hail as a masterpiece. The songs explored dark folk tales and the mystical side of the Russian Orthodox Church, incorporating traditional instruments like the accordion. The album was a metaphor for Russians’ searching for their post-Soviet identity, Mr. Gorbachev, the music journalist, said.

Some of Mr. Grebenshchikov’s phrases, drawn from his lyrics, have entered everyday language. Russians will interject “Rock 'n' roll is dead, but I am not” into a conversation, for example, to mean that life endures amid the struggle.

Mr. Grebenshchikov left Russia on a previously scheduled flight a day after President Vladimir V. Putin invaded Ukraine. He had already shifted his base to London from St. Petersburg, seeking to play with more varied musicians.

Married three times, with four grown children, he became a British citizen this year, making travel much easier for his roughly 60 concerts per year and decreasing the risk of arrest. From Istanbul to Riga to Chicago, he plays to countless fans who have fled Russia. For those still there, he regularly posts new songs on Instagram.

A heart attack a couple of years ago slowed him a little, but the spirit that first inspired Aquarium has not faded. As he says at one point in the movie, “I don’t think the need to rebel will ever go away.”

Alina Lobzina contributed reporting from London.

item.title: What to Know About the Rohingya Muslim Genocide Case at the World Court
item.description:
The International Court of Justice will rule on Thursday whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, a landmark decision years in the making that will have far-reaching implications.

If found guilty, Myanmar would be the first state — as opposed to an individual — held to account for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The African nation of Gambia brought the case against Myanmar to the court, the United Nations’ top judicial body, in 2019, with backing from the Organization of Islamic Cooperation. Since then, 11 other countries have formally lent their support to the case. The United States has already deemed the Myanmar security forces’ campaign of violence against the Rohingya, which culminated in a frenzy of killing, sexual violence and mass arson nine years ago, to be a genocide.

A guilty verdict against Myanmar could have bearing on another genocide case at the I.C.J.: South Africa’s claim against Israel for the violence in Gaza.

“This judgment is about much more than Myanmar,” said Matthew Smith, the chief executive officer of Fortify Rights, a nonprofit that has documented the plight of the Rohingya for nearly 15 years. “It’s a test of whether international law can deliver justice to people who have suffered the gravest crime imaginable.”

After Myanmar’s independence from Britain in 1948, the Muslim Rohingya were just one of the scores of ethnic groups in the country, which was then known as Burma. They won parliamentary elections, formed university student unions and ran big businesses. But in their home in western Rakhine State, they faced increasing repression from Buddhists from the Rakhine ethnic minority, as well as from the nation’s Bamar majority.

In 1982, the country’s military rulers codified their chauvinism, and the Rohingya were rendered essentially stateless. By 2012, they had lost their freedom of movement and assembly. Their calls to prayer were silenced; many could not attend school. Some were penned in internment camps. Others suffered village burnings and other pogroms, even before the attacks intensified in 2016 and 2017.

Various Myanmar governments, including one led by the Nobel laureate Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, have refused to even acknowledge the Rohingya as a legitimate ethnic group, referring to them instead as interlopers from neighboring Bangladesh.

In 2017, Myanmar’s security forces launched what were called “clearance operations,” after Rohingya militants attacked police posts and a military base. The collective punishment of the entire Rohingya population was swift and planned: Security forces, along with ethnic Rakhine mobs, rampaged through Rohingya communities, killing, burning and raping. About 400 villages were erased.

United Nations investigators said that 10,000 deaths from the “clearance operations” was a conservative figure. Rights groups say the perpetrators beheaded old men and herded women and children into buildings that they set on fire.

The massacres catalyzed the most rapid exodus of refugees in recent history, adding to an outflow to Bangladesh that had begun the year before. About 1.2 million Rohingya now crowd refugee camps, with no hope of returning home. Following Myanmar’s descent into full-blown civil war in 2021, much of the Rohingya homeland is now controlled by a Rakhine militia accused of killing hundreds of Rohingya. The Myanmar military has conscripted Rohingya.

Thousands of Rohingya have died during perilous sea crossings to Malaysia, where they work menial jobs. Human traffickers stalk the refugee camps. International aid has plummeted.

In 1948, following the Holocaust, the U.N. defined a new crime, genocide, as “acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.” Such acts include killing, causing bodily or mental harm and inflicting conditions that are calculated to bring about a group’s physical destruction.

Committing acts of cultural destruction, however, is not enough for such violence to be considered genocide. There must also be proven intent — and that, as the U.N. notes, is the hardest factor to determine.

“Everything the military did — killing us, raping our mothers and sisters, burning our villages, taking away all our freedoms — was to destroy the Rohingya people,” said Mohammed Furkhan, who fled Myanmar for Bangladesh in 2017 when his village was destroyed. “I hope the World Court says this is genocide, and the world community can find a solution for us,” he said, referring to the I.C.J.

The court does not have the power to enforce its rulings and may depend on support from the United Nations Security Council, which has two members — China and Russia — that would likely protect Myanmar.

Still, a verdict finding that the state committed genocide could set an important legal precedent. It could pave the way for determining reparations for Rohingya survivors. Myanmar could also be ordered to halt continuing violence against the Rohingya, but that is likely to be unenforceable.

Separately, the International Criminal Court, which takes cases against individuals rather than states, is considering a Rohingya genocide case against alleged top perpetrators, including U Min Aung Hlaing, the former military chief who is now the president of Myanmar.

item.title: Rio Tinto to Pay $250 Million to Address Mine’s Environmental Damage
item.description:
The multinational mining company Rio Tinto has committed to paying $250 million into a fund to address the long-lasting environmental and human rights consequences of a massive copper mine in Papua New Guinea.

The agreement announced this week arose from a complaint filed more than six years ago by residents living in the vicinity of Panguna mine in Bougainville, an autonomous region in the Pacific island nation. The claim was concerned with the effects of the Rio Tinto-controlled mine, which ceased operation in 1989.

Human rights and mining experts said the commitment was a rare instance of a corporation accepting responsibility for the impacts of a mine without being legally forced to do so. Community members from Bougainville, along with the Australian advocacy group Human Rights Law Centre, filed the complaint before a nonjudicial dispute resolution body in Australia, which does not have the ability to compel action by businesses.

Panguna mine, which was one of the largest in the world at the time, operated from 1972 to 1989 before conflict broke out, partly spurred by discontent that only a small fraction of the profits were benefiting the local community. The unrest led to a decade-long civil war.

While the mine was operating, an estimated 100,000 tons of waste rock, known as tailings, were released downstream each day, burying whole villages and completely altering the course of the Kawerong and Jaba river system.

The fund will go toward addressing safety and other issues in the river and delta areas, as well as social programs for the communities that have had their livelihoods affected by the mine for generations.

“The industry doesn’t have a track record in addressing a legacy like this,” said Deanna Kemp, director of the Center for Social Responsibility in Mining at the University of Queensland. “Remedying legacy issues of this size, scale and complexity have not been attempted before without the pressure of the law.”

Previous efforts to hold Rio Tinto legally responsible in U.S. courts had been dismissed on jurisdictional grounds. The company walked away from its stake in the mine in 2016. A new operator, an Indian mining company, has been brought in as a partner by the separatist region’s autonomous government to redevelop the mine.

Theonila Roka Matbob, whose family has lived for generations a short distance downstream from the mine, said that even though there is still a long process ahead to address the mine’s aftereffects, she was heartened by the establishment of the fund and the effect it would have on the community’s children. Ms. Matbob, a former representative for the region in Bougainville’s Parliament, was central in the effort to organize the community and to bring the complaint against Rio Tinto.

“It’s a step toward building a different future,” she said. “Obviously, no amount of money will restore the environment to what it was, but at least this is a genuine commitment by Rio Tinto.”

She said the agreement also represented some justice for her 85-year-old grandmother, who was briefly jailed in the 1960s for protesting the mine before it opened.

Keren Adams, legal director for the Human Rights Law Center, said that even though there was hard work ahead, the agreement was a breakthrough moment for the estimated 25,000 people who have been living with the environmental and social consequences of the mine.

“While it may not fix everything, it is going to make a transformative difference to lives along the mine,” she said. “For communities to have gotten them back to the table, gotten them to commit to a significant contribution to fix the environmental damage that they left, that’s highly unusual, especially outside a court process.”

A representative for Rio Tinto said in a statement that the agreement was an “important milestone” and said that the company remained “committed to working with communities to shape the activities supported by the fund.”

Even though it took decades of persistence from the community, the outcome was a good sign that mining giants may be coming to terms with their social responsibility, said Justine Nolan, director of the Australian Human Rights Institute at the University of New South Wales in Sydney.

“It’s an unprecedented process and amount,” she said. “It’s Rio recognizing it has dues to pay this community.”

item.title: These Villagers Wonder if They’re on the Front Line of Russia’s Shadow War
item.description:
For years, Helmut Rost rode his bike to the edge of the Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany to pick dandelions for his rabbits. Then one recent summer, he was startled to find a police officer yelling at him to stop.

Mr. Rost, a retiree, said the officer gave him a verbal warning to stay at least nine feet from the airport fence. “I had been doing it for years and the security people never did anything,” he said.

But ever since an odd explosion at the airport in 2024, a new reality has settled over the nearby villages, one that was compounded with the discovery in August of an explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane there. The German authorities have blamed Russia for the failed drone attack, among the gravest recent claims of Russian subterfuge in Europe. Russia denied involvement.

The state police now patrol the airport’s outer perimeter, federal officers patrol inside the airport, where they operate drone jammers, and some residents in neighboring villages are constantly thinking about what else could happen.

There have been other worrisome episodes in Germany, like drone overflights, threats to the lives of defense company executives and guns found stashed that have been linked to Russia.

But it is the near miss at Leipzig/Halle airport — which is named for two nearby cities — that has made the strongest impression on Germans. Security and military officials now use the airport as a byword for clandestine Russian attacks in Germany, one of the primary targets of Russia’s so-called hybrid campaign of sabotage against Ukraine’s allies in Europe.

Mr. Rost, who lives in Freiroda, a village next to the airport, chuckled as he recalled his brush with the law. He belongs to a camp of residents who have chosen to take a light view of the potential new risks.

But not everyone feels that way.

“It’s not like we are constantly looking in the sky, but of course we’re not completely carefree either — we’re not,” Sven Hösel, 55, who runs a popular restaurant in the center of Glesien, a village that abuts the airport’s northern runway. “One does perceive it as a real danger, but one just tries to deal with it normally.”

Mr. Hösel’s restaurant, Gasthof Ennewitz, serves as a meeting spot for people living near the airport. He said that another recent episode, in which two men drove into the airport fence by accident and fled the scene, had prompted a fresh round of conversations about safety.

Like others, Mr. Hösel said many in the community were worried that the accident at the fence had not been noticed right away, despite all the scrutiny. The authorities began investigating after discovering a gaping hole in the barrier. The case was solved when the two men turned themselves in. “You’d think they have alarms on the fence or cameras,” Mr. Hösel said.

A spokesman for the airport said that it complied with all international and national regulations when it comes to ensuring the safety of the perimeter.

Many of the nearly 20,000 people living in the villages around the runways have been there for decades and have become inured to the inconveniences of living next to a major airport. Instead, they focus on the positives: nature, space, easy public transport to Leipzig and — when vacation time comes around — easy access to holiday destinations.

Most people I spoke with were more likely to complain about the noise from the nightly takeoffs of DHL cargo planes than the fact that the airport has become a main character in an escalating global standoff.

The most frequent complaint is that the airport is now operating fewer passenger flights, curbing the airport’s positive economic impact on the local area as well as reducing its community outreach programs, like a program that funded soundproof windows for nearby residents.

But while the passenger terminal is less busy, the cargo terminal has gradually become the second busiest cargo airport in Germany behind Frankfurt. DHL, Amazon Air and a Ukrainian cargo company called Antonov Airlines are based here.

In July 2024, a DHL parcel containing an incendiary device caught fire. Because of a delay to the flight scheduled to carry it to its destination, the parcel ignited while still on the ground, preventing a catastrophic midair explosion. Western intelligence officials later concluded that the episode was a Russian test run.

This summer a bus driver found an explosives-laden drone lying just yards from one of the Ukrainian Antonov planes. Security cameras later revealed that the drone had initially hit the gigantic plane’s wing. If the explosive had functioned as designed, it would have caused the fuel in the wings to explode, security services said, very likely blowing up the entire plane. Weeks after the first drone was found, Germany’s interior minister said authorities had found proof linking that attack to Russia.

This month, the national police asked the public to help find a person who they believe was involved in the drone attack. Besides handing out fliers and posting it online, the police have put up several huge “wanted” posters featuring an A.I.-generated image of a man in a hoody on an electric bicycle next to roads close to the airport.

The problem, some residents say, is that the airport has become a resupply hub for Ukraine.

“Times have changed, and this airfield has essentially become a military transit hub,” said Michael Walde, 65, a teacher living in the area. “That’s why it has become vulnerable,” he added. Mr. Walde said that the only solution would be to ban any weapons or military goods from transiting at that airport, which he notes is designated a civilian airport.

“This is how global politics works,” he said. “Because we sit at a key junction, we are at its mercy.”

Sylvia Schimpf, 54, who runs the local council, said that each time something happens, the community talks about it for a week or two, but then most move on. Some people, she conceded, think about it constantly.

While nobody denies that there have been multiple major incidents at the airport, not everyone believes the official explanation that Russia is behind them.

“Opinions are certainly divided on that,” said Mr. Hösel, the restaurateur.

Many residents grew up during the Cold War, when the area formed part of the Soviet-allied East Germany, and some have sympathy for Moscow.

Others dismiss the idea that the incidents so far have posed much threat.

“I’m not scared,” said Helmut Lehmann, another resident. If someone actually wanted to cause damage to the airport, he said, they’d only have to drive down the road “and use their shotgun to shoot at one of the fuel tanks.”
