item.title: Leaders of China and Japan Meet Amid Political Feud
item.description:
The atmosphere was tense. The handshake was quick.

President Xi Jinping of China and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan met briefly on Wednesday at the opening of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, China, their first encounter since the start of a bitter diplomatic feud a year ago.

Mr. Xi offered Ms. Takaichi a slight smile as she made her way to a banquet with other world leaders. He did not appear to respond when she said a few words to him, before they posed for a photo with Mr. Xi’s wife, Peng Liyuan.

Experts said the interaction was unlikely to signify any serious thaw in relations, which have been at a low point since China reacted furiously last year to a comment Ms. Takaichi made about Taiwan.

Tetsuo Kotani, a professor at Meikai University in Chiba Prefecture in Japan, said that Ms. Takaichi seemed “eager to make the most of this opportunity” in Shenzhen. Mr. Xi, he said, “maintained a businesslike demeanor.”

“I don’t think there’s any hope this time around for improved relations,” Mr. Kotani said.

As the summit got underway, there were reminders of the frosty state of relations. While other world leaders received warm welcomes at the Shenzhen airport — a crowd of dancing young people with flowers greeted the South Korean leader, for example — there were no such gestures for Ms. Takaichi, according to Japanese news reports.

The dispute began last year, when Ms. Takaichi, a longtime critic of China, told Japan’s Parliament that any attempt by Beijing to blockade or seize Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, implying a potential military response. Beijing considers Taiwan, a self-governed democracy, part of its territory.

China unleashed a wave of reprisals against Japan, urging tourists to avoid the country, limiting the export of critical minerals and restricting Japanese seafood imports. At the same time, Chinese officials and commentators have hardened the language they use to describe Japan, with some seeking to belittle Ms. Takaichi by omitting her title in official settings.

China’s punishments have started to squeeze Japan. The decline in tourism has hurt sales at some duty-free stores, hotels and restaurants. Japan could soon run low on supplies of some rare earths — minerals used to make a range of essential technologies, from M.R.I. machines to drones — according to analysts.

Chinese officials and scholars have suggested that anything short of Ms. Takaichi retracting her comment on Taiwan would not satisfy Mr. Xi.

Shao Yuqun, director of the Institute for Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau Studies at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said that Mr. Xi was responding in part to intense anger among the Chinese public over Ms. Takaichi’s remark.

Ms. Shao added that finding a way to improve relations with Japan was “certainly not the priority” in Shenzhen.

Ms. Takaichi has been working to accelerate Japan’s defense buildup to counter a volatile security environment, including threats from China, North Korea and Russia.

There is little appetite among the Japanese public to curry favor with Beijing and Ms. Takaichi is unlikely to give in to Chinese demands to retract her remark on Taiwan. As she enters her second year in office, she enjoys relatively robust public support, and won a historic supermajority in the lower house of Japan’s bicameral Parliament in February.

The meeting had echoes of an encounter in 2014, when Mr. Xi offered an icy handshake to Shinzo Abe — then Japan’s prime minister and a mentor to Ms. Takaichi — at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing during another moment of tension between the two countries. Mr. Abe was eventually able to get more time with Mr. Xi, and relations between the two countries improved somewhat.

After their encounter on Wednesday, Mr. Xi and Ms. Takaichi are unlikely to have an extended meeting in Shenzhen, officials from both countries said.

Ms. Takaichi is expected to face another challenge on Thursday: a potential sit-down on the sidelines of the summit with Russia’s president, Vladimir V. Putin. The meeting would take place as Mr. Putin is escalating pressure on Japan. He recently seized Russian assets of Japan Tobacco, detained a Japanese journalist and visited islands claimed by both Moscow and Tokyo.

Japan will also be watching the outcome of a first-ever trilateral gathering of the leaders of the United States, China and Russia.

Tobias Harris, the founder of the advisory firm Japan Foresight, said Tokyo hopes the meeting is “light on substance.”

“You can’t rule out the eventual possibility of some attempts at a big grand settlement that is prejudicial to the global order that Japan prefers,” he said.

item.title: Carney and Trump Hold Unscheduled Trade Meeting at Asia Summit
item.description:
Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada has advanced his goal of reducing Canada’s economic reliance on the United States during a weeklong swing through Asia, emerging with trade deals with China and the Philippines.

But he was also presented with an unexpected opportunity to improve relations with Washington. On Wednesday, Mr. Carney announced that he would meet with President Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, leaving open the prospect of Canada starting to mend the rift with its neighbor.

“We have long said, and believed and still believe, that there is a mutually beneficial agreement between Canada and the United States in the context of the new U.S. trade policy,” Mr. Carney told reporters. “We’ll have discussions on that. And, we will do what’s necessary in order to achieve that deal, but only if that deal that is in the interest of Canadians.”

Hours later, Mr. Carney’s office issued a brief statement confirming that the two leaders met and “discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement.” It offered no details.

Before Wednesday, Mr. Carney’s aides said there was no expectation of a meeting with Mr. Trump in China. At the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in South Korea last year, the two men only spoke informally during a dinner.

How much progress, if any, will result from the meeting is unclear. Before the encounter, Mr. Carney described dealing with the Trump administration on trade as a “two steps forward, one step back type thing.”

Since his return to office, Mr. Trump has imposed a variety of tariffs on a wide range of Canadian products. While those tariffs have been effectively suspended for many goods that qualify as being made in North America, the suspension has not applied to the key auto, steel and aluminum industries. Their products face tariffs of up to 50 percent.

Negotiations between the two countries collapsed in August with each side pointing fingers at the other for the failure.

At the beginning of this month, Mr. Carney said that talks would restart after Mr. Trump said the United States would back off on some secondary issues that were irritants for Canada, including requirements relating to the promotion of Canadian and French language content on digital streaming services.

There has been little apparent activity since then but Mr. Carney said on Wednesday that “we have been making progress.”

Much more obvious has been the progress Mr. Carney has made with China. Before he took office, diplomatic incidents — including what was widely seen in Canada as the hostage-taking of two Canadians by China in 2018 — and Canada’s decision to follow the United States with 100 percent tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles had brought relations between the two countries to a near standstill.

But this week, at his second formal meeting with President Xi Jinping of China this year, Mr. Carney walked away with a second reduction in Chinese tariffs aimed at a variety of farm and fish products. The deal effectively marked the end of the trade war sparked by the auto tariff, Mr. Carney said, opening the door to an expanded trade relationship between the countries.

Mr. Carney also repeated this week that if Canada were unable to persuade Mr. Trump to end tariffs on its auto exports, it would look to China, Japan and Europe to keep Canada’s auto industry afloat.

That suggestion drew criticism from Peter Navarro, a senior adviser to Mr. Trump.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.?” Mr. Navarro said in a social media post. “This is offensive in the extreme. You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive — as it is already doing.” Pete Hoekstra, Washington’s ambassador to Canada who has frequently offended Canadians, shared the post.

On Wednesday, however, Mr. Carney dismissed suggestions that Canada’s renewed relationship with China was poisoning its economically vital relationship with the United States.

“In my conversations with the president, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” Mr. Carney said. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”

But selling the benefits of China back home may not be so easy. A recent poll found that only 14 percent of Canadians want closer trade ties with China. By contrast, 58 percent back Mr. Carney’s push for a closer relationship with the European Union.

After noting that Canadian fishermen and farmers strongly favor more trade with China, Mr. Carney downplayed the extent of the trade relationship.

“Relative to many other countries, our trade with China is quite modest and the breadth of it is quite modest.”

item.title: Russia Vows to Rebuild Destroyed Crimea Bridge. It Could Take Years.
item.description:
Russian officials on Wednesday vowed to restore “within a tight time frame” the only bridge linking mainland Russia with Crimea after an elaborate Ukrainian attack knocked out its main roadway span. But restoration work is likely to take years.

It was the fourth time since Russia’s all-out invasion in 2022 that Ukraine managed to strike the structure, which is both symbolically and logistically important. After those earlier attacks, repairs took months. This time, the damage is far more extensive. Some Ukrainian officials questioned whether rebuilding would be possible at all with the threat of further attacks.

The steel arch that crashed into the sea early Tuesday after a Ukrainian drone and missile attack was the most complex element of the structure, known as the Kerch Strait Bridge.

Perched over a shipping channel, the nearly 750-foot-long arch was installed in October 2017, three years after Russia illegally annexed Crimea. It elevated the roadway more than 100 feet above the channel so cargo ships and other vessels could pass between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

The steel components were produced over several months at a factory in the Russian city of Voronezh. They were then welded together over roughly 11 months on a coastal slipway near the strait before being floated out on catamaran pontoons. It took several more months to connect the arch to the rest of the bridge and pave a road across it.

Andreas Kappos, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at Khalifa University in Abu Dhabi, said that “about two years is a reasonable time for restoring traffic on the road bridge.” But that’s only if construction is not interrupted by Ukrainian strikes and if the piers supporting the arch span were not seriously damaged, he said.

Donald O. Dusenberry, a consulting engineer who has investigated bridge failures, said that simply clearing the debris would be a complicated job. He also noted that the single arch span was not like the repeatable spans that made up a majority of the bridge and could be fairly easily replaced. And if the piers must be repaired, that would add yet another layer of complication, he said.

Even so, Russia is likely to pour substantial resources into the reconstruction, given its significance to President Vladimir V. Putin and his government.

On Wednesday, Russia dispatched vessels, including one that could be used to clear debris, to the site of the attack, according to VesselFinder, a ship-tracking service.

The $4 billion bridge is a symbol of what Russia calls its “irreversible” control over Crimea. More broadly, it is a monument to Mr. Putin’s ambitions.

The Russian leader has linked his own image to the bridge, personally opening the roadway in May 2018 by driving a construction truck across it.

That was only part of the fanfare. A contest chose the bridge’s “official song” from more than 2,500 submissions, according to organizers. A feature film portrayed a love triangle against the backdrop of its construction. Russian pop stars performed at a concert marking its completion. The Russian central bank minted a special coin depicting the two main steel arches, and the Russian postal service issued a stamp celebrating the opening.

The bridge has become an equally potent symbol for Ukraine. In 2022, after Ukrainian forces struck the bridge for the first time, crowds lined up in Kyiv to buy their own postage stamp — one depicting the bridge in flames.

When it was built, the roadway bridge — together with a parallel railway bridge that remains open — provided the only direct land link between Russia and Crimea.

After the full-scale invasion in 2022, Russian troops captured a major overland highway linking Russia with Crimea. Over the past few years, Moscow has expanded the highway, restored damaged railways in the region and built new rail lines running to Crimea.

But compared with the bridge, those routes lie closer to the front line, making them more vulnerable to Ukrainian drone strikes. Last summer, Ukraine ramped up such attacks, disrupting traffic along the highway.

The roadway of the Kerch Strait Bridge has been a vital route for residents of Crimea and mainland Russia who traveled for tourism. Many Crimeans also drove across it to buy cheaper groceries in Russia’s neighboring Krasnodar region.

The bridge was used less often to supply the Russian war effort, military analysts said. Russia had curtailed its use for that purpose after the earlier Ukrainian attacks.

In October 2022, an explosion caused two sections of the road span to collapse and set fuel tankers ablaze on the parallel railway. It took Russia roughly four and a half months to reopen the highway and nearly seven months to complete repairs on the railway.

In July 2023, a Ukrainian naval drone attack caused one section to collapse and knocked another loose. It took Russia nearly three months to restore full traffic on the bridge.

Marc Santora contributed reporting.

item.title: Iran Fires Missiles and Drones at Gulf Arab States as Peace Talks Falter
item.description:
Kuwait and Bahrain said that they had intercepted Iranian aerial attacks on Wednesday as peace talks between the United States and Iran stalled and uncertainty lingered in the region over whether a new round of fighting would erupt.

The Iranian military said that it had fired drones at a Kuwaiti air base, aiming for U.S. air-defense systems and launch platforms, Iranian state media reported. The Kuwaiti foreign ministry denounced the attack, the first Iranian offensive against the country in about two months, saying that it was a dangerous escalation that threatened regional stability. It was unclear whether the attack caused damage.

Bahrain, an island nation in the Persian Gulf that is home to the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet, said it had also been attacked on Wednesday. The Bahraini authorities have reported several attempted Iranian attacks since Friday. On Sunday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said that the Iranian military had targeted a radar system at a Bahraini air base.

The Middle East has been in limbo for months as talks between the United States and Iran have failed to reach a sustainable resolution to the war. Gulf Arab countries, which host vast American military installations and thousands of U.S. troops, have received the brunt of Iran’s retaliatory attacks since the United States and Israel began their war with Iran in February.

Those attacks had largely petered out as the conflict entered a stalemate. But with the war deadlocked and few signs of progress toward a durable peace agreement between the United States and Iran, tit-for-tat strikes have resumed.

Iran has also continued to go after ships in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway that is a crucial shipping route for Gulf oil exports. On Wednesday, ADNOC Logistics and Services, a subsidiary of Abu Dhabi’s state oil company, said that one person was missing and 11 were injured after one of its vessels was attacked the previous day while sailing through the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran’s leaders have hardened their negotiating position with the United States since President Trump’s setback in the midterm elections, which were partly seen as a rebuke of his handling of the war, according to American, European and Iranian officials.

The United States has sent more military assets to the Middle East in recent weeks, and it struck Qeshm Island in Iran this month in what American officials said was a defensive measure. American and Israeli military officials have also drawn up plans for renewed strikes that would most likely target energy infrastructure and other sites vital to the Iranian economy, according to U.S. officials and other people briefed on the deliberations.

Several Gulf countries have lobbied against another round of fighting and pushed for a comprehensive deal to end the war. Qatar is mediating between the United States and Iran.

“It is not in the interests of the region to go through another round, and indeed not the interests of Iran to go through another round, of confrontation,” Anwar Gargash, a senior Emirati official, said at the Manama Dialogue security conference in Bahrain this month.

“We in the United Arab Emirates are looking for a political solution to this crisis,” he added. “We don’t believe that military solution is viable.”

item.title: Israeli Tanks Advance Across Gaza Cease-Fire Line in Rare Incursion
item.description:
Israeli forces advanced on Wednesday into an area of the central Gaza Strip controlled by Hamas, making a rare incursion into territory outside the area held by Israel since a U.S.-brokered cease-fire agreement was reached at the end of last year.

The Israeli military said that its troops, conveyed by tanks, moved into the area with engineering machinery to destroy Hamas infrastructure that “threatened Israeli forces” in a joint operation with the Shin Bet, an Israeli intelligence agency.

The military added that the raid was a limited effort, suggesting that a large assault was not underway, but it did not offer details on what was being targeted or how long the operation would last.

Earlier Wednesday, the Israeli Air Force struck Nuseirat in the central Gaza Strip, killing at least one person, according to a statement from the Al Awda Medical Complex, which said it also treated two people injured in the strike. The Israeli military said the strike targeted a Hamas commander and was separate from the ground operation.

Ahead of the incursion, the Israeli military issued evacuation orders to residents of the area, saying Israeli vehicles would be traveling along Salah al-Din Road, a main artery, and it would be closed to Palestinians.

Hamas called the Israeli actions “a blatant violation of the cease-fire agreement” and said that by “herding citizens into a narrow strip of the territory,” Israel was making a humanitarian catastrophe worse.

Mahmoud Basal, a spokesman for Gaza’s civil defense, an emergency service under the Hamas-run interior ministry, said that more than 5,200 people were displaced by the Israeli operation.

While Israel has often carried out airstrikes in Gaza since agreeing with Hamas to halt the war, the incursion marked the first time Israel has deployed heavy armored vehicles far across the cease-fire line separating the areas under Palestinian control from those held by the Israeli military.

More than 1,600 people have been killed by Israeli fire during the cease-fire, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.

Many Palestinians in Gaza hoped Israel would cease its aerial attacks after Hamas agreed in July to an American framework for decommissioning and storing weapons, intended as the first step toward rebuilding the war-torn coastal enclave. But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said the plan fell short of true disarmament and refused to halt the strikes, which at times have come daily.

Though the Israeli military said the ground operation is limited, Palestinians said they worry it might signal that Israel is increasing its attacks.

“I thought my life was over,” said Muhammad Yasin, 50, who works at a bakery on Salah al-Din Road, recalling the moment he saw a cloud of dust kicked up in the distance by Israeli tanks and heard gunfire.

He said he and about 40 family members then fled their tent for another camp. “We really hoped this war was over for us already,” he said.

item.title: Voters Are Punishing Autocrats. But Many Still Embrace Them. Why?
item.description:
With so many citizens revolting against the threat of autocracy, reshaping the politics of Brazil, India, Serbia and the United States, it might look like liberal democracy is recovering from the past decade’s authoritarian onslaught.

But autocracies still outnumber democracies. Far more people live under authoritarian governments than not. And for millions, strongman rule remains deeply appealing.

The philosopher Thomas Hobbes argued that it’s because citizens see tyrants as protectors. Hannah Arendt believed that the lonely and lost seek purpose in totalitarianism. Some social scientists suggest that much of humanity is simply predisposed to demand “oneness and sameness.”

But what if another force is also at play?

New research in psychology has strongly linked support for authoritarianism to an innate belief that the world is hierarchical, with countries, people, ideas — even animals — scaled from worst to best.

For those who tip from simply seeing hierarchy to insisting on its enforcement, embracing a strongman can seem logical. What rivals may see as malice, they see as fighting with their “team” in the inescapable battle against what researchers describe as “an abyss of unimportance.”

“It reframes where authoritarianism is coming from,” said Jer Clifton, 41, a senior research scientist at the University of Pennsylvania who has studied beliefs about the world for more than a decade. “It’s like, do you care about your family? Do you care about your community?”

Political scientists fix their gaze elsewhere, prioritizing structural forces such as media control, or evidence that political elites shape public attitudes.

But instead of looking top-down at how leaders manipulate the masses, Dr. Clifton and others are exploring the phenomenon from the bottom up.

Eventually, they believe their work could help us change how people view the nature of the world and our polarizing differences, undermining authoritarianism and leading to a broader embrace of the humility and tolerance that underpins democratic values.

Dr. Clifton’s studies identify a hierarchical worldview as one of several “primal beliefs” — fundamental assumptions about how each of us sees life.

A few primals, as he and others in the field call them, are relatively well-known. The belief in a just world and belief in a dangerous world have been studied for decades. But Dr. Clifton, who grew up mostly in Asia as a son of Christian missionaries, set out as a graduate student at the University of Pennsylvania in 2012 to build an inventory of them all.

Eventually, he identified 26 primal beliefs. Martin Seligman was his adviser. Considered the father of positive psychology, a 30-year effort to shift psychology’s focus from mental illness to well-being, Dr. Seligman described the research into primal beliefs as “an entirely new field” that draws inspiration from cognitive behavioral therapy.

CBT, as it is known, equips people with practical skills to change how they think about themselves. Primals researchers are testing whether people’s beliefs about the world can also be changed.

“That’s kind of the great challenge,” Dr. Seligman said. “If they’re changeable, this matters a great deal politically, personally, and for therapy.”

Several studies have shown that primal beliefs are correlated with behavior. In shooting simulations, for example, the belief that the world is dangerous was tied to a higher likelihood of firing on someone who was unarmed in a split-second reaction.

An earlier generation of psychologists maintained that right-wing authoritarianism was also driven by fear of a dangerous world. Terrified of violence and disorder, people seek safety in iron-fisted rule — an idea as old as Plato.

But when Dr. Clifton and his frequent research partner, Nicholas Kerry, 44, a British political psychologist, tested for a wider range of primal beliefs, they found a more potent motivator: the belief that hierarchy defines the world.

In a 2023 study, they discovered that while liberals and conservatives generally saw the world equally in terms of safety, people who self-identified as conservatives were far more likely than liberals to agree with statements like: ‘‘Things are rarely equal. Most plants and animals, and even people, are better or worse than one another.’’

For some, that can lead to anti-democratic tendencies. New research from Dr. Clifton, Dr. Kerry and four other psychologists showed that belief in a hierarchical world was, by a large margin, the strongest predictor of support for authoritarianism.

Among thousands of study participants from the United States, the United Kingdom, Italy and South Korea, there was a strong connection between seeing rank in everything and support for an “uncompromising team captain,” willing to bend or break democratic rules to defend the so-called natural order.

“Be it people, ideas, species, whatever,” Dr. Kerry said. “It all seems to cluster around this broader idea that some things are more important, more valuable and better than others.”

Erica Frantz, a political scientist at Michigan State University who studies authoritarianism, connected the discussion back to disputes over the Enlightenment.

“There was this idea that traditional society is best, hierarchy is best, and there’s a natural way of things,” she said. “Theorists say this was a response to liberalism and the threat that it posed to aristocracy and monarchy.”

In the 20th century, signs of a shared hierarchical-authoritarian mind-set were everywhere.

Thousands of Germans gathered in beer halls to hear Hitler argue, throughout the 1920s, that a natural elite must rule.

The Fascist leader Benito Mussolini of Italy and Joseph Stalin of Soviet Russia also consolidated power with tiered social systems, rewarding conformity in ideology and social behavior, including gender roles.

Political science points directly at such tactics. “Savvy authoritarians are able to generate political support by tapping into some sort of societal divide,” Dr. Frantz told me.

But psychology suggests that autocrats and their supporters are also glued together by a shared conviction that certain people and ideas are simply superior and must remain on top.

Once identified, the demand for a simple, predictable order suddenly seems common.

In China, Communism and beliefs about the supremacy of the Han ethnic majority have layered newer hierarchies over Confucian ideas of respect for authority.

In Russia, the Kremlin enforces order internally while President Vladimir V. Putin has said that all nations fit two categories: “Either a country is sovereign, or it is a colony.”

Hierarchy similarly runs through President Trump’s foreign policy. By making Stephen Miller his new chief of staff, Mr. Trump has promoted a pugilist who also describes life as an unavoidable fight for rank.

The “real world,” he said earlier this year, is governed by the strong over the weak, adding “these are the iron laws of the world.”

Running through all these examples: the notion that inequality is normal, fated, not worth opposing unless you’re naïve.

“The more people see the world in terms of hierarchies,” said Steven Levitsky, a Harvard political scientist who has studied authoritarianism in dozens of countries, “the less good it is for democracy.”

When we met in Philadelphia, Dr. Clifton emphasized that hierarchical worldviews do not automatically lead to authoritarianism. Being conservative or believing the world has sharp distinctions of worth does not make you a tyrant or a supporter of one.

He cited his uncle, a pastor and “the kindest person on the planet.”

“He sees the world as an extremely competitive and cutthroat place but refuses to participate in that perceived brawl for spiritual and ethical reasons,” Dr. Clifton said. “Likewise, you can see the world as a very hierarchical place — see hierarchy as the reality — but simply refuse to live your life in reaction to that perception for various other reasons.”

Reducing the power of worldviews to influence people’s actions, Dr. Clifton hopes, could increase our tolerance for one another so we can bridge political divides.

An inkling of promise comes from a study published this year. Researchers (including Dr. Clifton) asked Republicans who endorsed the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol insurrection to take photos for 10 days of people, places or things that they valued. Then they wrote about how their snapshots “represent only a few of the many things and people in the world that matter.”

The exercise helped participants recognize that what’s meaningful is not absolute or limited by their own preferences. Afterward, they recorded a decrease in their willingness to endorse or engage in political violence compared with a control group.

Dr. Clifton says the goal is to teach us “how to hate people less.”

Jennifer McCoy, a political scientist at Georgia State University and global expert on how to reduce polarization, said the study and the research on hierarchical thinking were “useful contributions, and provide some hope.”

Dr. Clifton considers the results a first step toward adjusting primal beliefs. His dream is to develop educational means to encourage greater tolerance, starting in schools or with children’s books.

The most fundamental ways people see the world “go unchanged mainly because nobody is trying to change them,” Dr. Clifton told me. “You can’t call a mountain ‘unclimbable’ just because nobody knew about the mountain and had never tried to climb it.”
